title: Evernote Pricing in 2026: What Each Plan Costs
summary: Evernote pricing has Free, Starter, and Advanced plans. To choose between them, focus on monthly storage limits rather than the cost difference.
body_markdown:
## Evernote capture automation with Activepieces


Activepieces can send your emails, form responses and app data into Evernote on their own, and how many flows you create is never what it charges for: its pricing page lists unlimited flows on every plan from Free through Ultimate, and only runs spend credits, at 1 credit a run.


So one small flow per source, one for email, one for forms, one per app, costs nothing extra to keep, whereas Zapier charges a task for each action and Make a credit for each module, so the tidy version gets dearer every time it runs.


It does nothing to Evernote's limits or price, so every note it creates's still a note you pay for in space.


That second part matters more than the first. Automation's a faster way to fill a free plan, and a faster fill means you reach the limit sooner.


If you were going to hit a wall in a year by typing notes by hand, a workflow can bring that wall much closer without you noticing.


### What can be automated into Evernote


Activepieces works by "flows". You pick something that starts it (a new email, a submitted form, a change in another app), and it then carries out steps you set, ending with a new note in a notebook you choose.


Its Free plan includes 1,000 credits a month, enough for 1,000 such runs, which is twenty times Evernote's 50-note cap, leaving Evernote's restriction as the real bottleneck.


You build this by connecting boxes on a screen, not by writing code, and you can run it on your own server or use the company's hosted version.


Look at the picture below for the usual shape: three sources feed one workflow, which writes into a single notebook, and the counter on the notebook's the number to watch.


Three sources, one workflow and one notebook's also how people end up with a full account. Each source adds notes at its own pace, and the notebook counts them all together, so the counter climbs faster than any one source suggests.


### Automated notes still count against limits


Whether a machine made the note makes no difference to Evernote. A form response saved at 3 a.m. uses the same allowance as a page you typed yourself.


A flow that saves every email in an inbox spends that allowance on messages you may never reopen.


So treat the workflow like any other spending decision, and count before you build it:


1. Estimate how many notes each source will create in a typical month.
2. Add those together and compare the total with the limit you are closest to.
3. Narrow the trigger, for instance to emails with a certain label or forms of one type, until the total fits.


If the narrowed total still crowds your plan, that's the useful finding. It tells you which limit forces your upgrade, and that, not the monthly price, is the figure to choose a tier by.
